guide.bridge: Entry point: you need a computer and browser. No programming, terminal or security vocabulary is assumed. A phone can read lessons, but later coding labs need a computer.
guide.teaching:
A file is a named collection of data. A folder groups files and other folders. A path tells you where a file is stored: cyber-notes/week1.txt means week1.txt inside cyber-notes. The extension is a naming convention, not proof of what a file contains. Turn on filename extensions in your file manager so week1.txt and week1.txt.exe are distinguishable.

A browser retrieves pages from addresses called URLs. In https://example.org/lesson, https is the scheme, example.org is the host, and /lesson is the path. A downloaded file is a separate local copy. Closing a browser tab does not delete that copy; editing the local copy does not change the website.

Create a dedicated learning folder and use invented data throughout the course. Keep a plain-text learning log recording the date, question, action and result. When a later lesson mentions an artifact, it means a saved output such as a script, screenshot or report that another person could inspect. Always test recovery, rather than assuming that a visible Save message proves a backup exists.
guide.example:
cyber-notes/
  week1.txt
  copies/
    week1-backup.txt

week1.txt contents:
Question: Where is my work saved?
Action: Created a local text file.
Result: Reopened it after closing the editor.
guide.explanation: Use your system's file manager to create cyber-notes and its copies subfolder. Open a plain-text editor, type the three log lines and save as week1.txt inside cyber-notes. Close the editor, locate the file in the file manager and reopen it. Copy it into copies as week1-backup.txt. Change only the original and reopen both: their contents should now differ. This demonstrates the difference between a copy and a live synchronised document.
guide.exercise: Create the shown folder tree. Add a fourth line to the original: Next: learn account safety. Keep the backup unchanged. Record the full location shown by your file manager, the extension and the difference between the two files. No terminal is required.
guide.solution: The original has four lines and the backup three. Both reopen from the file manager. Your answer identifies the containing folder, not only the filename. If both changed, you edited the same file or a shortcut rather than creating an independent copy.
guide.challenge: Without the walkthrough, create a separate practice2 folder with an original note and a recovery copy. Close every editor, find both files and demonstrate which is the newer copy. Explain the scheme, host and path of https://example.org/course/start.
guide.challenge_solution: An independent copy survives closing the editor. For the URL: scheme https, host example.org, path /course/start. A convincing submission gives file locations and observed contents; a screenshot of an open unsaved editor is insufficient.

O01.concept: A computer stores information in files, groups files in folders, and runs programs that interpret those files. A plain-text editor saves the characters you type; a word processor also saves formatting. A filename extension is a convention that helps software choose an interpreter. Renaming notes.txt to notes.py does not turn a paragraph into a working Python program.
O01.mechanism: A local path describes a location on a filesystem. A URL identifies a resource using a scheme such as https, a host, and a path. Downloading a resource creates a local copy; editing that copy normally does not change the remote resource. Keep your learning work in one folder so that experiments and evidence can be found again.
O01.example: Create cyber-learning with notes, code, and evidence subfolders. Save a sentence as notes/first-lesson.txt. Close the editor, find the file using your file manager, and reopen it. Download a course handout into evidence. Record its original URL beside the local filename. You now have both the artifact and its provenance.
O01.pitfall: An icon or filename alone does not establish what a file contains. Check the full name and open unfamiliar files with an appropriate viewer.

check.question: Which action changes the remote course handout?
choices: Renaming your downloaded copy
Moving your downloaded copy into another folder
Editing it through a service where you have permission to update the original
check.explanation: A download is a separate copy. Local file operations do not modify the server's original.

guide.bridge: Builds on O01: files and browser addresses. You do not need any attack tools.
guide.teaching:
Security begins with the asset and the permitted action. Confidentiality asks who may read data, integrity asks who may change it, and availability asks whether authorised people can use it when needed. One action can affect all three. A leaked backup harms confidentiality even if the primary service stays online.

Permission must cover the particular system, technique, time and data involved. Owning a laptop does not grant permission to test every service that laptop can reach. A designated training lab provides a scope; read it before starting and stop if a redirect or instruction takes you outside it. Publicly readable is not equivalent to authorised for intrusive testing.

A useful scope document states the owner, exact targets, allowed actions, forbidden actions, time window and reporting route. It also states a stop condition, such as encountering real personal information. When uncertain, preserve a minimal description and ask the owner instead of collecting more data. The exercises here use fictional scopes and do not require contacting or testing any external system.
guide.example:
Fictional scope
Owner: local training instructor
Target: offline folder cyber-notes/training
Allowed: read and edit the supplied text files
Excluded: other folders, accounts and network services
Window: this practice session
Stop: any real personal information appears
Report: write a local incident note
guide.explanation: Reading a supplied training file is within scope. Opening a sibling folder called payroll is outside scope even if the operating system permits it. Deleting training files might technically be an edit, but conflicts with the intent if destructive work was not agreed; seek a clearer scope. Finding personal data triggers the stop condition before further exploration.
guide.exercise: For this exact scope, classify five actions: read training/readme.txt; edit training/answer.txt; open ../payroll.csv; scan example.org; stop after finding a real phone number. For each give permitted, prohibited or stop, plus one sentence tying the decision to scope.
guide.solution: Read and edit are permitted within the stated training directory. Payroll and the scan are prohibited. The phone number requires stopping and a minimal local report. No network action is necessary to answer.
guide.challenge: Write a scope for an invented local note-taking app. Include six boundaries and a stop condition. Explain which security goal is harmed by (a) revealing a private note, (b) changing its owner, (c) making notes unavailable.
guide.challenge_solution: The goals are confidentiality, integrity and availability respectively. The scope needs owner, targets, allowed actions, exclusions, window and reporting route. It must not imply that permission for a local app covers its third-party hosting or identity provider.

O02.concept: Security means preserving properties that matter to someone. Confidentiality limits disclosure, integrity limits unauthorised change, and availability keeps a service usable when needed. These goals can conflict: disconnecting a server may reduce disclosure while preventing legitimate access. Begin with the asset, its owner, and the unwanted outcome rather than a favourite security tool.
O02.mechanism: Permission defines where practical testing belongs. A training lab grants a limited scope; a public website being reachable does not grant permission to test it. Write down the systems, activities, accounts, and time window allowed by your own lab or an explicit authorisation. Stop when the exercise crosses that boundary. Use synthetic data, not real credentials or personal records.
O02.example: Model a family photo archive. Confidentiality means only selected people can view photos. Integrity means files cannot be silently replaced. Availability means a failed laptop does not destroy the only copy. Create a table with one failure and one control for each property, then identify which failures remain possible.
O02.pitfall: A discovered weakness does not expand your permission. Keep evidence minimal and follow the lab or owner's reporting process.

check.question: A lab permits testing one provided virtual machine. What is in scope?
choices: That virtual machine under the lab's stated rules
Other machines on the same network
The provider's production login service
check.explanation: Scope attaches to the explicitly authorised systems and activities, not to everything technically reachable.

guide.bridge: Builds on O02: assets, threats and authorised scope. Use fictional account details; never put recovery codes in this notebook.
guide.teaching:
An account connects an identity to capabilities. A password is one authentication factor; a second independent factor reduces dependence on that password. A passkey can also resist common phishing flows by binding authentication to a site. Recovery is part of authentication: a weak recovery email can bypass a strong primary login.

Start with an inventory: service, importance, recovery route, multi-factor status and last backup test. Record status, not secret values. Prioritise email and the password manager because they often unlock other accounts. Update devices, lock screens and restrict extensions because account security also depends on the endpoint that handles the session.

A backup should survive the failure you care about. A file copied to the same disk helps with accidental editing but not disk loss. Synchronisation may replicate a deletion, so it is not automatically a historical backup. Choose a retention period, keep an independent recovery copy and restore a harmless file to verify your process. Privacy adds a separate question: even if a service protects data, does it need to collect that data at all?
guide.example:
Fictional inventory
Service        Importance   MFA       Recovery     Restore test
Demo email     high         enabled   offline kit  not applicable
Local notebook medium       device    spare copy   2026-10-29
Photo archive  medium       account   email        not tested

Do not include passwords, real recovery codes or session tokens.
guide.explanation: The photo archive is marked not tested, so it is a recovery risk even if a backup tool reports success. The demo email has higher priority because it recovers the archive account. An offline recovery kit needs protected storage; the inventory should say where the process is documented without exposing the secret itself.
guide.exercise: Using invented services, make three inventory rows. Copy a harmless note to a separate recovery location, remove only a disposable working copy, then restore it. Record original contents, restored contents and what failure your copy would not survive.
guide.solution: The restored contents match. A same-disk copy does not survive disk failure. The inventory contains no authentication secrets. A good explanation links the recovery chain from one service to another.
guide.challenge: A fictional laptop and its disk are lost. Email recovery codes existed only on that laptop; a cloud folder synchronised deletions. Identify two independent recovery weaknesses and propose a test for each.
guide.challenge_solution: Use protected recovery material accessible without the lost laptop, and a versioned/independent backup whose retention survives deletion. Test sign-in recovery with a safe planned procedure and restore an invented file from a historical version; never disable your only working factor as a casual experiment.

O03.concept: An account links a person or service to permissions. A password is one way to prove control of that account; a second factor adds a different proof. A password manager helps create and store distinct passwords, reducing the damage when one service leaks a credential. Recovery methods also grant access and deserve the same attention as the normal login.
O03.mechanism: Updates reduce exposure to known defects. Device locking reduces casual access. Backups recover information after loss, but only if the copies survive the same failure and can be restored. Synchronisation alone can replicate an accidental deletion. Privacy starts by asking what information is collected, who can access it, and how long it is retained.
O03.example: Choose a harmless document. Back it up to a separate location, modify the working copy, and restore the earlier version into a new folder. Compare contents. Next draw the recovery path for a test account: what happens if the primary device is lost? Store recovery codes securely rather than in a public notebook.
O03.pitfall: A backup job reporting success is not proof of recovery. A restore test supplies stronger evidence.

check.question: Which observation best supports a backup's usefulness?
choices: The backup application displayed a green icon
A separate copy was restored and its contents checked
A synchronisation folder exists on the same disk
check.explanation: A verified restore tests the recovery outcome; a status icon tests only part of the process.

guide.bridge: Builds on O01. Review addition, multiplication and division before the binary examples. No calculus is used.
guide.teaching:
A positional number uses a base and place values. Decimal 47 is 4×10+7. Binary 1011 is 1×8+0×4+1×2+1=11. One bit has two possible values; eight bits form a byte with 256 possible patterns. A pattern needs an interpretation: the same byte can represent an integer, part of text or an instruction.

Hexadecimal groups four bits into one digit. The digits after 9 are A through F, representing 10 through 15. To convert a byte, split it into two groups of four bits. This makes hex a compact way to inspect data without claiming that those data are text.

Algebra describes relationships rather than particular values. If cost=quantity×price, dividing both sides by a nonzero quantity gives price=cost/quantity. Logarithms reverse exponentiation: log2(8)=3 because 2 cubed is 8. Security uses these ideas when reasoning about search spaces. Encoding is a representation rule, not secrecy: anyone who knows the rule can reverse it. Unicode code points and UTF-8 bytes are related but not interchangeable counts.
guide.example:
Binary       Place values              Decimal  Hex
0010 1010    32 + 8 + 2                 42       2A
0100 0001    64 + 1                     65       41

2^4 = 16, so four bits have 16 patterns.
ASCII/UTF-8 letter A is byte 0x41.
UTF-8 letter é uses bytes C3 A9, not one byte.
guide.explanation: For 2A, convert 2 to 0010 and A to 1010, then join. The value is 2×16+10=42. For A as text, 65 is its code point and one-byte UTF-8 value. For é, the code point is U+00E9 but UTF-8 uses two bytes. A length limit must say whether it counts characters, code points or bytes.
guide.exercise: Convert 13 and 31 to eight-bit binary and two-digit hex. Solve 3×x=21. Calculate log2(32). Explain whether converting a message to hex protects confidentiality.
guide.solution: 13=00001101=0D; 31=00011111=1F; x=7; log2(32)=5. Hex does not protect confidentiality because decoding needs no secret.
guide.challenge: Convert binary 11110000 to decimal and hex. A field allows at most four UTF-8 bytes: do the strings AAAA and ééé fit? Explain every step without relying on a calculator result alone.
guide.challenge_solution: 11110000=128+64+32+16=240=F0. AAAA uses four bytes and fits. ééé uses six UTF-8 bytes and does not. A character-count limit of four would make a different decision.

M01.concept: Binary and hexadecimal are ways to write numbers, not encryption. In decimal, 507 means 5×100 + 0×10 + 7. Binary uses powers of two, so 1011 means 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Hexadecimal uses sixteen symbols, 0–9 and A–F; one hex digit represents four bits. A byte has eight bits and can represent 256 distinct patterns.
M01.mechanism: The same bits can represent an integer, text, an instruction, or a colour depending on the interpretation. An encoding defines that interpretation. Units matter too: bits and bytes differ by a factor of eight. Logarithms reverse exponentiation; log2(8)=3 tells us that three binary choices select among eight outcomes. Algebra lets us rearrange performance and risk equations without guessing.
M01.example: Convert decimal 13 to binary 1101 and hex D. Write a byte as 00001101 and observe that its value is unchanged by leading zeros. Then compare 10 megabits per second with 10 megabytes per second using the stated decimal units. Explain every conversion, including units, in your notebook.
M01.pitfall: Hexadecimal-looking text is not evidence that information is protected. Encoding is reversible without a secret.

check.question: How many distinct patterns fit in four bits?
check.explanation: Each independent bit doubles the possibilities: 2×2×2×2 = 16.

guide.bridge: Builds on M01 arithmetic and O01 files. Install Python 3 using the linked CS50 setup, or use its documented browser environment. Commands below assume python3 is available.
guide.teaching:
A program is a sequence of instructions. A variable gives a name to a value; assignment stores a value under that name. In Python, price=100 does not prove a timeless mathematical equality: a later assignment can change price. A function packages instructions that can be reused with different inputs.

A definition starts with def, a function name, parentheses for parameter names and a colon. Indented lines form its body. A parameter is the local name used inside a function; an argument is the actual value supplied by a call. return sends a result back to the caller. print displays a value; displaying and returning are different operations.

Type the whole example into lesson.py, preserving indentation. Save it in your learning folder, open a terminal there and run python3 lesson.py. If your system uses python instead, follow the setup guide and record that command. A terminal command runs the saved file, so save changes before rerunning. If you see a traceback, read the final error line and locate the named file/line before editing randomly.
guide.example:
# lesson.py — four spaces indent the function body
def add_tax(price, rate):
    tax = price * rate
    total = price + tax
    return total

result = add_tax(100, 0.2)
print(result)
# Run: python3 lesson.py
# Expected: 120.0
guide.explanation: The definition creates a function; it does not calculate tax yet. The call binds price to 100 and rate to 0.2. tax becomes 20.0, total becomes 120.0 and return passes 120.0 to result. print then displays it. If return is omitted, the call returns None even if the function prints a number. Floats approximate decimal numbers; this is a teaching example rather than a production money calculation.
guide.exercise: Create lesson.py exactly as shown and run it. Add calls for (50,0.1), (80,0) and (0,0.2). Predict all outputs on paper first. Then explain what happens if you write print(add_tax) instead of print(add_tax(50,0.1)).
guide.solution: The additional results are 55.0, 80 and 0.0 (numeric formatting can reflect the input types). print(add_tax) displays a function representation rather than calling it. Your evidence should include the saved code, run command and a trace of one call.
guide.challenge: Without copying the function body, write apply_discount(price, fraction) that returns price minus price×fraction. Test (200,0.25), (75,0), (40,1). Explain one input restriction a real application should enforce.
guide.challenge_solution: A correct body is return price - price * fraction. Results are 150.0, 75 and 0. A real design should decide allowed price types/ranges and restrict fraction to 0 through 1; simply accepting arbitrary values can create nonsensical totals.

P01.concept: A variable gives a name to a value. A function groups instructions behind a name, accepts inputs called parameters, and may return a result. Calling a function executes its body; defining one does not. Python values have types, so the string '12' and the integer 12 behave differently even when they print similarly.
P01.mechanism: Follow data through a program in small steps. Input enters as text, conversion produces a number, a calculation produces another value, and output displays it. Keep calculation separate from interaction so the calculation can be tested with several inputs. A return value belongs to the caller; printing sends text to an output stream and is not a substitute for returning data.
P01.example: Define add_tax(price, rate) to return price * (1 + rate). Call it with 100 and 0.05 and record the returned 105. Then call it with 0 and with a second rate. Write down the value and type of every argument. Decide explicitly how invalid input will be handled instead of letting accidental conversions define the behaviour.
P01.pitfall: A variable name does not enforce a type or a unit. Use meaningful names and validate values at boundaries.

check.question: A function prints 5 but has no return statement. What does its caller receive in Python?
choices: None
The integer 5
The string '5'
check.explanation: Printing and returning are different actions. A Python function without an explicit return value returns None.

guide.bridge: Builds on P01 function calls and M01 arithmetic. Use Python 3; no additional package is needed.
guide.teaching:
A condition evaluates to True or False and selects a branch. Python uses == for comparison and = for assignment. An if/elif/else chain chooses the first matching branch. Indentation determines which statements belong to it. Check boundaries explicitly: x>0 and x>=0 disagree exactly at zero.

A loop repeats a body. The useful way to understand it is to record the state before and after each iteration. In a for loop, the iteration variable takes each item in order. An accumulator such as total carries information across iterations. A return exits the whole function immediately, not just the current loop iteration.

Tracing is an independent prediction, not a description written after running the program. Make a table with item, condition result and total. Include an empty input: it tests whether the initial state already supplies a sensible result. Include negative and repeated values so a mistaken branch or reset does not hide behind one happy-path example.
guide.example:
def positive_total(items):
    total = 0
    for value in items:
        if value > 0:
            total = total + value
    return total

# Trace [2, -1, 3]
# before: total=0
# value=2: True  -> total=2
# value=-1: False -> total=2
# value=3: True  -> total=5
# return 5
guide.explanation: Initialisation occurs once, before the loop. The negative item leaves total unchanged. If total=0 were moved inside the loop, previous contributions would be erased. If return total were indented inside the loop, the function would stop after the first item. These are distinct faults and need different test inputs to reveal.
guide.exercise: Trace positive_total for these six supplied sequences: []; [0]; [2,-1,3]; [-2,-3]; [4,4]; [1,-1,1]. Record one row per iteration and the final output. Run the program only after all six predictions.
guide.solution: Outputs in order: 0, 0, 5, 0, 8, 2. The empty list has no iterations and returns the initial zero. Zero is excluded by >0 but adding it would not change this particular sum; distinguish branch behaviour from final-output equivalence.
guide.challenge: Write nonnegative_count(items), counting values >=0. Trace it for []; [-1,0,2]; [0,0]; [-3]; [5,-5,5]; [1,2,3]. Then change >= to > and identify which tests distinguish the versions.
guide.challenge_solution: Counts: 0,2,2,0,2,3. The [-1,0,2] and [0,0] cases change under >. A correct implementation increments count by one, rather than adding the value. Show traces and explain why empty input is valid.

P02.concept: A condition chooses a branch; a loop repeats a block. An if/elif/else chain selects the first true branch. A for loop visits items in an iterable. A while loop continues while its condition remains true, so its body must make progress toward an exit when termination is intended. Indentation determines which instructions belong together.
P02.mechanism: Trace a program using a table with one row per iteration. Record the current input, variable values, condition result, and output. This makes off-by-one errors visible. In Python, range(3) produces 0, 1, 2: the upper bound is excluded. An algorithm is the sequence of steps; code is one expression of those steps in a particular language.
P02.example: Start total at zero and loop over [2, 4, 6], adding each item. Your trace should show totals 2, 6, and 12. Next count values greater than 3, keeping the count separate from the sum. Test an empty list and a list containing only 3 to make the boundary rule explicit.
P02.pitfall: A loop that works on one example may still fail on empty input or at a boundary. Trace those cases deliberately.

check.question: How many times does a Python for loop over range(3) execute its body?
choices: Two
Three
Four
check.explanation: The values are 0, 1, and 2. Excluding 3 does not exclude 0.

guide.bridge: Builds on P02 branches and loops. Run the Python example locally using invented records.
guide.teaching:
A list stores an ordered sequence; an index selects a position starting at zero. A dictionary maps keys to values. These are different contracts: records[0] asks for the first list item, while record["name"] asks for a field. Choose a structure that matches the question your code must answer.

Input data can be malformed without the program being malicious. A missing key raises KeyError; converting nonnumeric text with int raises ValueError. Catch the expected error near the operation you can recover from. Catching every exception and silently continuing can hide programming defects and make a partial result look complete.

Separate validation from computation. First decide the accepted shape and types. Then collect valid values and explicit rejected records. Retaining rejection reasons makes later analysis auditable. Do not modify the input list while iterating through it unless the algorithm is deliberately designed for that behaviour.
guide.example:
records = [{"name":"a", "count":"2"},
           {"name":"b", "count":"bad"},
           {"name":"c"}]
accepted, rejected = [], []
for index, record in enumerate(records):
    try:
        count = int(record["count"])
    except (KeyError, ValueError):
        rejected.append(index)
        continue
    accepted.append(count)
print(sum(accepted), rejected)
# 2 [1, 2]
guide.explanation: Index 0 converts successfully and adds 2 to accepted. Index 1 fails conversion, while index 2 lacks the key. Both follow the explicit rejection path. continue advances to the next item. This example assumes each record is a dictionary and count is convertible text; a full input contract should validate those assumptions too.
guide.exercise: Use the exact three records above. Add {"name":"d","count":"0"} and {"name":"e","count":"-1"}. Change validation to reject negative counts with a recorded reason. Report accepted sum and rejected indices.
guide.solution: Accepted counts are [2,0], sum 2. Rejected indices are [1,2,4]. Negative rejection must be a deliberate rule after conversion, not a blanket exception. The original input list remains unchanged.
guide.challenge: For records [{"count":"3"},{"count":"3"},{"count":"x"}], return both the total and a frequency dictionary of accepted counts. Explain why repeated keys in a dictionary cannot represent two independent records by themselves.
guide.challenge_solution: Total is 6; frequencies can be {3:2}; index 2 is rejected. A dictionary has one value per key, so assigning the same key again replaces its previous value unless the value is an explicit collection or count.

P03.concept: Choose a collection according to the question it must answer. A list preserves a sequence; a dictionary maps keys to values; a set represents distinct members. Modifying a collection can affect every reference to that same object. Copying a variable name does not necessarily copy the underlying data.
P03.mechanism: Data modelling means deciding what a record means before processing it. A login event might have an account, timestamp, and outcome. Missing fields and invalid values are different problems from an empty event list. Exceptions signal exceptional failures; catch the specific failures you can handle, and preserve useful context rather than silently treating every error as success.
P03.example: Represent three synthetic login events as dictionaries in a list. Count failures per account with another dictionary, and collect distinct accounts in a set. Add a malformed record. Decide whether to reject it or report it separately. Check that your answer does not change merely because the events arrive in a different order.
P03.pitfall: A broad exception handler that returns an empty result can hide corruption and make failed analysis look like a clean system.

check.question: You need one count per account name. Which collection directly models this?
choices: A string containing all account names
A single Boolean
A dictionary mapping account names to counts
check.explanation: The account name is a key and the count is its associated value. This is a dictionary's natural relationship.

guide.bridge: Builds on P03 data structures and error handling. Python includes csv, json and datetime; install no extra packages. Save the Python program as convert_events.py, not csv.py or json.py, so its filename does not shadow a standard-library module.
guide.teaching:
A file is a byte sequence; text decoding interprets those bytes using an encoding. Specify UTF-8 rather than depending on the machine default. A context manager written with with closes a file even when an error interrupts the block. Relative paths are resolved from the process working directory, which may differ from the script directory.

CSV describes rows and columns but does not automatically assign numeric types. JSON can represent objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Parse data with their format libraries instead of splitting lines at commas: quoted fields can contain commas. Validate the parsed shape before relying on it.

Time values need a reference. A timestamp ending in Z means UTC; a numeric offset allows conversion to UTC. A timestamp without an offset is ambiguous unless a surrounding contract supplies a timezone. Distinguish event time from the time a collector received the event. Sorting strings with mixed offsets does not reliably sort actual instants.
guide.example:
# Save events.csv as UTF-8:
# time,count
# 2026-01-01T10:00:00+01:00,2
# 2026-01-01T09:30:00+00:00,3
import csv, json
from datetime import datetime, timezone
with open("events.csv", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
for r in rows:
    r["count"] = int(r["count"])
    r["time"] = datetime.fromisoformat(r["time"]).astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat()
print(json.dumps(rows, indent=2))
guide.explanation: The first event is 09:00 UTC, so it precedes the second at 09:30 UTC. count is converted from text to an integer. The resulting JSON preserves numeric meaning rather than storing every value as a string. Create events.csv without the comment prefixes shown in the example.
guide.exercise: Create the supplied CSV and run the conversion. Add a third row 2026-01-01T08:45:00+00:00,4. Sort parsed events by UTC time, write events.json with UTF-8 and reload it. Report ordered counts and total.
guide.solution: Order is 4,2,3; total 9. The reloaded value is a list of three objects with integer counts. The UTC time of the first original row is 09:00, not 10:00.
guide.challenge: Process two supplied timestamps: 2026-02-01T12:00:00+02:00 and 2026-02-01T09:30:00+00:00. Which comes first? Explain how you would handle a third value 2026-02-01T10:00:00 with no timezone.
guide.challenge_solution: 09:30 UTC comes before 10:00 UTC. Reject the offset-free value or apply an explicitly documented source timezone; do not silently assume the reviewer's computer timezone.

P04.concept: A module packages related Python definitions for reuse. Files persist data after the program exits. CSV represents rows and columns; JSON represents nested values such as objects, arrays, strings, and numbers. A parser turns encoded text into program values. Parsing successfully does not establish that the resulting values are valid for your application.
P04.mechanism: Separate reading, validation, analysis, and writing. Use a context manager to close files reliably, specify the text encoding, and handle malformed data explicitly. Timestamps need a timezone or an unambiguous convention. A local clock reading such as 01:30 can be ambiguous during a clock change; an offset-aware timestamp is safer for joining evidence from different systems.
P04.example: Read a small JSON array of synthetic events. Require account, outcome, and an offset-aware time. Reject an event missing its outcome and report the count of rejected records. Write a CSV summary of valid events. Reopen your output to confirm headers, row counts, and non-ASCII account names survived the round trip.
P04.pitfall: A valid JSON document can still contain impossible values, unexpected types, or missing required fields.

check.question: What should follow successful JSON parsing at an application boundary?
choices: Validation of the expected structure and value constraints
Immediate trust in every value
Removal of all error handling
check.explanation: A parser verifies the format's grammar. Application validation checks whether the data makes sense for its intended use.

guide.bridge: Builds on P04 files and P02 branches. Tests below use Python's built-in unittest; no network or model calls are involved.
guide.teaching:
A test makes a claim about observable behaviour. Good cases distinguish a correct implementation from realistic mistakes. For a boundary n>=3, test 2,3 and 4 rather than only 100. A test can pass while missing a defect if the chosen inputs never reach the relevant branch.

When debugging, first reproduce the failure with the smallest useful input. Compare expected and observed values, then trace the first point where they diverge. A debugger lets you pause and inspect state; a print can also help if it answers a specific question. Add a regression assertion after the fix so the same behaviour remains checked.

Regular expressions describe text patterns, not arbitrary structured formats. fullmatch requires the whole string to match, while search can find a matching substring. In a simple identifier pattern, brackets form a set of allowed characters, + repeats one or more times and a quantifier applies to the immediately preceding pattern. Length and character policy should be intentional.
guide.explanation: The first character must be a lowercase letter. It is followed by two through seven lowercase letters or digits, making total length three through eight. abc! is rejected because fullmatch does not ignore the trailing exclamation mark. A search-based implementation would accept a matching substring and violate the contract.
guide.exercise: Run the supplied tests. Temporarily replace fullmatch with search in your disposable file and record the failing case. Restore the implementation and add cases for uppercase input, a space and an empty string.
guide.solution: abc! exposes the search mistake. ABC, a b and the empty string are rejected under this policy. Restoring fullmatch makes all expected cases pass. A valid identifier is not by itself proof of authorisation.
guide.challenge: Define valid_port(text) accepting only decimal text whose numeric value is 1 through 65535, with no spaces or sign. Supply tests for "0","1","65535","65536","-1"," 80" and "x".
guide.challenge_solution: Accept "1" and "65535"; reject the others. Validate the text syntax first, then convert and check range. Explain whether non-ASCII decimal characters are allowed by your chosen predicate; an ASCII-only regex [0-9]+ makes the policy explicit.

P05.concept: A test states an expected behaviour and checks it repeatedly. Start with ordinary inputs, then boundaries, invalid values, and previously failing cases. A useful assertion would fail if an important behaviour broke. Debugging asks why observed behaviour differs from expected behaviour; reduce the case, inspect values, and test one hypothesis at a time.
P05.mechanism: Regular expressions match patterns in text. Anchoring, character classes, repetition, and escaping control what matches. A pattern search is not equivalent to validating an entire field. Complicated patterns can also behave poorly on hostile input, so prefer simple bounded formats or dedicated parsers when the data has an established grammar.
P05.example: Write a function that accepts only a synthetic account label of 3–12 lowercase ASCII letters. Test a valid label, two letters, thirteen letters, digits, and a trailing newline. Use full-string matching. Deliberately remove the length limit and confirm that a test fails; this checks that the tests actually protect the requirement.
P05.pitfall: Passing tests establish behaviour only for the cases and properties tested. They are evidence, not a universal proof.

check.question: A validator must check the entire input. Which approach fits?
choices: A search for any matching substring
A full-string match against the allowed format
Accepting any input that contains one letter
check.explanation: A substring match can ignore unwanted prefixes or suffixes. Full-string matching checks the whole field.

guide.bridge: Builds on O01 files. Use the linked Linux shell environment or a local Linux/macOS terminal. Windows learners can use the documented course Linux environment; do not paste shell syntax into an unrelated shell.
guide.teaching:
The shell reads a command, identifies its arguments and starts a program. The prompt is not part of the command. pwd prints the current directory; ls lists entries; cd changes the current directory for later commands. An absolute path begins at the filesystem root. A relative path begins at the current directory, and .. refers to its parent.

Spaces separate arguments unless quoted. The path "first note.txt" is one argument when quoted and two when unquoted. Quoting prevents unintended splitting; it does not grant access or make a destructive command safe. Before changing files, inspect your current directory and operate only inside the practice tree.

Documentation is a tool, not a memory test. Use a command's manual or --help to inspect its options. Output and errors are different streams; later lessons combine them. Read the entire message when an operation fails: a missing path and a permission denial have different causes and should not trigger the same fix.
guide.example:
mkdir -p cyber-shell/copies
cd cyber-shell
pwd
printf 'hello\n' > 'first note.txt'
cp 'first note.txt' copies/backup.txt
ls -l
cat copies/backup.txt
# Expected content: hello
guide.explanation: mkdir creates only the named practice tree. The redirection > writes printf output to a file and replaces existing contents at that path, so choose a fresh directory. cp creates an independent copy. After cd copies, cat ../"first note.txt" reaches the original through the parent directory. Record the actual pwd output rather than assuming every machine uses the same home path.
guide.exercise: Run the commands inside a fresh learning directory. Enter copies, print pwd, display ../"first note.txt", then return to its parent with cd .. (two dots). Explain what the parent component means and how the working directory changes.
guide.solution: From copies, cd .. returns to cyber-shell. Both displayed files contain hello. The absolute pwd path ends in the expected directory. A command written cd ... normally names a literal directory called ... and is not parent traversal.
guide.challenge: Without the example, create a folder named second lab containing a text file and a copies subfolder. Copy the file, access it using a relative path from copies, and explain which command changes future relative-path resolution.
guide.challenge_solution: Correct quoting keeps second lab as one path. cd changes the working directory. A reproducible answer includes the directory tree and actual read-back contents, not just successful exit status.

L01.concept: The shell reads a command line and starts programs. The working directory is the location from which relative paths are interpreted. An absolute path begins at the filesystem root; a relative path begins at the current directory. The shell and the file manager operate on the same files, even though their interfaces differ.
L01.mechanism: Learn pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, cp, mv, and the relevant help pages before combining destructive operations. Spaces and special characters have shell meanings, so quote paths that must remain a single argument. A command's output and exit status answer different questions: output carries data, while a conventional zero exit status indicates success.
L01.example: In a disposable practice folder, create a directory named case notes. Enter it using a quoted path. Save a text file, copy it, and compare the two copies. Use pwd before each operation and explain how the same relative filename would resolve from a different working directory. Keep removal exercises inside this disposable folder.
L01.pitfall: A command copied from a tutorial may assume a different working directory. Confirm the target before changing files.

check.question: From /tmp/lab, where does the relative path notes/a.txt resolve?
choices: /notes/a.txt
/tmp/notes/a.txt
/tmp/lab/notes/a.txt
check.explanation: A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory, here /tmp/lab.

guide.bridge: Builds on L01 command arguments and P02 conditions. Use a disposable Linux/macOS practice directory and your own unprivileged account.
guide.teaching:
Each process has input, output and error streams. A pipe connects the standard output of one program to the standard input of another. It does not automatically include errors. An environment variable supplies inherited configuration to child processes; a shell variable need not be exported.

Unix permissions distinguish owner, group and others, with read, write and execute bits. For a directory, execute means traversing it; it does not mean running the directory as a program. Process identity and directory permissions both affect access. Adding broad permissions to make an error disappear can create an unintended boundary change.

A script should state its interpreter, quote variable expansions and check failures. Shell commands can return nonzero statuses without printing a dramatic error. A pipeline's status rules depend on the shell, so do not infer that every stage succeeded from the final filter alone. Start with simple explicit checks and harmless files before automating multi-stage operations.
guide.example:
# Save count.sh; run sh count.sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
folder='shell-data'
mkdir -p "$folder"
printf 'ok\nfail\nok\n' > "$folder/events.txt"
count=$(grep -c '^ok$' "$folder/events.txt")
printf 'ok count: %s\n' "$count"
chmod 600 "$folder/events.txt"
ls -l "$folder/events.txt"
# count: 2; owner read/write only
guide.explanation: Quotes ensure the folder variable remains one argument. grep -c counts matching lines, not occurrences within one line. chmod 600 grants owner read/write and no permissions to group or others. This does not prove that a privileged administrator cannot read the file; the threat model matters.
guide.exercise: Run the script with the exact three event lines. Add a line okay and confirm ^ok$ does not count it. Explain the difference between NAME=value and export NAME=value, then inspect a harmless exported variable in a child shell.
guide.solution: The count stays 2. Anchors constrain the complete line. An exported variable is inherited by a newly started child process; an ordinary shell variable is not automatically inherited. Do not use a real secret as the demonstration value.
guide.challenge: A practice directory has mode 700 and a contained file mode 644. Explain whether an unrelated unprivileged user can reach the file through that directory. Propose an owner-only mode for a new private file and describe a verification step.
guide.challenge_solution: Directory traversal is denied to unrelated users despite the file's read bits. 600 is an owner-only file mode. Check both parent-directory traversal and the file mode; use an explicitly controlled second account only if available, rather than assuming ls proves all access paths.

L02.concept: A process is a running program with an identity, environment, and open resources. Unix permissions describe access for an owner, group, and others. Directory execute permission means traversal, rather than running the directory. Permission checks depend on identities and path components, not just the final file's mode.
L02.mechanism: Pipes connect one program's standard output to another's standard input. Standard error remains a separate stream unless redirected. Environment variables pass configuration to child processes and can influence program behaviour. A shell script turns a sequence into a repeatable procedure; quote variable expansions, check failures, and avoid interpreting untrusted data as shell syntax.
L02.example: Create a harmless text file with owner-only permissions and inspect its mode. Build a pipeline that selects synthetic failed-login lines and counts them. Send an intentional error to a separate file and compare it with standard output. Write a script accepting one quoted filename; verify it works when the path contains spaces.
L02.pitfall: Changing a file to executable does not grant the permissions needed to read its inputs or traverse its parent directories.

check.question: What does a pipe normally connect?
choices: One process's standard output to another's standard input
Every file on disk to the next process
Only the first process's standard error
check.explanation: The ordinary pipe operator transfers standard output. Standard error needs a separate redirection if it should join that stream.

guide.bridge: Builds on P05 tests and L02 processes. Use Python 3 and its built-in venv module.
guide.teaching:
An object combines state with operations on that state. A class describes how objects are created. self refers to the particular instance handling a method call; two instances can have independent values. Shared mutable class attributes behave differently and can accidentally connect users that should be isolated.

A dependency environment separates project packages from system packages. Create it with python3 -m venv .venv, activate using the platform's documented command and verify which interpreter runs. Installing a package globally because an import failed can alter other projects. Record Python version and package versions so another learner can recreate your environment.

Reproducibility includes inputs and commands as well as versions. A dependency lock is not a security audit: it identifies what you installed, while vulnerability and provenance checks ask different questions. For this first object exercise, no third-party packages are required, so you can reason about instance isolation without network setup.
guide.example:
class Notebook:
    def __init__(self):
        self.entries = []
    def add(self, text):
        self.entries.append(text)

a, b = Notebook(), Notebook()
a.add("first")
print(a.entries, b.entries)
assert a.entries == ["first"]
assert b.entries == []
# Expected: ['first'] []
guide.explanation: Each constructor creates a new list. a.add changes only a.entries. Moving entries=[] to the class body would share that list unless an instance later replaces it, causing cross-instance leakage. The assertions test the intended isolation, not merely whether the method can be called.
guide.exercise: Create a venv, record python --version and run the shown program. Add a second entry to b and prove a stays unchanged. Record your activation and run commands. Do not commit the .venv directory.
guide.solution: a remains ["first"] and b becomes ["second"] when b.add("second") is called. Both isolation assertions should pass in a newly created environment with no additional packages.
guide.challenge: Write a Counter class with increment() and value starting at zero. Create two counters, increment one twice and the other once. Explain a test that would detect accidental shared state.
guide.challenge_solution: Final values must be 2 and 1. Checking both values after every increment detects a shared class-level mutable container or shared backing object. Record the interpreter and command so the result can be reproduced.

P06.concept: An object combines state with operations on that state. A class defines a pattern for constructing such objects. Use this when several values and behaviours belong together, rather than wrapping every function in a class. Understand the difference between independent instances and shared state before using classes to model security events.
P06.mechanism: A virtual environment separates a Python project's installed packages from other projects. It does not isolate the operating system like a virtual machine. Record the Python version, dependency constraints, setup instructions, and a minimal test. Reproducibility requires more than installing whatever versions happen to be newest today.
P06.example: Create an EventCounter class whose instances each maintain their own count. Instantiate two counters, update one, and assert that the other stays at zero. Run the test inside a fresh virtual environment. Document installation and execution so another learner can repeat the result without borrowing your existing environment.
P06.pitfall: A virtual environment is dependency isolation, not a safe boundary for executing malicious programs.

check.question: Two independent counters unexpectedly share a mutable list. What should you inspect first?
choices: The monitor's refresh rate
Whether the source file has comments
Whether the list was defined as shared class state
check.explanation: A mutable class attribute can be shared across instances. Per-instance state should be initialised for each object.

guide.bridge: Builds on L01 paths and P06 a small local project. Git tracks files; GitHub hosting is optional for this local exercise.
guide.teaching:
Git stores snapshots connected by history. The working tree is what you edit. The index, also called staging, selects content for the next commit. A commit records the staged snapshot, author information and a message. Saving a file in an editor does not stage it, and staging does not create a commit.

Use status and diff before each commit. Stage explicit paths so unrelated notes, environment folders or secrets are not swept into history. A later deletion does not remove a secret from earlier commits. If you ever expose a real secret, revocation and a deliberate history cleanup are separate tasks.

Branches are names pointing to commits. A merge combines histories and may need human conflict resolution. In this course, use a local disposable repository to learn conflicts; do not rewrite a reviewed team's history as a shortcut. A lab notebook should record why a change was made and how it was verified, not only the command list.
guide.example:
mkdir git-lab
cd git-lab
git init
printf 'first version\n' > note.txt
git status --short
git add note.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m 'docs: Add practice note'
printf 'second version\n' > note.txt
git diff
# Requires a locally configured Git author identity.
guide.explanation: Before staging, note.txt is untracked. After git add, its exact contents are in the index. The commit captures first version. The later edit appears in git diff but not in that existing commit. If author identity is missing, follow Git's setup documentation; the failure does not mean the file disappeared.
guide.exercise: Perform the shown local history. Stage the second version, inspect the staged diff and commit it. Use git log --oneline and git show to find the two versions. Record each commit's purpose in a separate nonsecret lab log.
guide.solution: Two commits show first version followed by second version. A clean status after the second commit means no current unstaged/staged edits, not that the history lacks sensitive material.
guide.challenge: In the disposable repo, create two branches from the same commit and make different edits to the same line. Merge them, resolve the conflict to a deliberate final sentence and record both parent commits. Explain how you verified the final content.
guide.challenge_solution: A conflict is expected for competing edits to one line. Keep the desired sentence, remove conflict markers, stage the resolved file and commit the merge. Verify git log --graph and the final file. Do not run reset or force-push against a shared project as part of this exercise.

L03.concept: Git records snapshots of tracked files in commits. The working tree contains current files; the staging area selects what the next commit will contain. A commit message explains the change, while the diff shows the exact content. Version history supports investigation because you can compare states and identify when behaviour changed.
L03.mechanism: A repository should help another person reproduce your work. Include setup instructions, dependency information, test commands, and evidence references. Ignore generated caches and local secrets before adding files. Deleting a secret in a later commit does not erase earlier copies from history; credentials that have been exposed need replacement through the issuing system.
L03.example: Create a repository for a tiny parser. Commit the working version, change one validation rule, and inspect the diff before staging that file. Make a second commit with a clear explanation. Use git log and git show to recover the reasoning and content of the first version without guessing from today's files.
L03.pitfall: A repository backup and a progress backup solve different problems. Your browser notebook is not automatically committed with your code.

check.question: What determines which current changes enter the next Git commit?
choices: All files currently open in the editor
The staging area
The names in the last commit message
check.explanation: Git commits the staged snapshot. Unstaged working-tree edits remain outside that commit.

guide.bridge: Builds on M01 arithmetic and P02 tracing. Read the notation here before the formal lecture; no proof-writing experience is assumed.
guide.teaching:
A proposition is a statement with a truth value. AND requires both statements to be true; OR requires at least one; NOT reverses a truth value. An implication P implies Q rules out the case where P is true and Q false. It does not assert that Q implies P. This distinction appears in access-control policies and proofs.

A set is a collection of distinct elements. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its codomain. A graph has vertices and edges; a directed edge records direction. A state machine adds states and transitions, allowing you to reason about every permitted next step rather than one observed execution.

A proof explains why a claim follows from assumptions. For an invariant, show it holds initially and that each permitted transition preserves it. Induction follows the same structure: establish a base case, assume a claim for an arbitrary step and prove the next. One successful test is evidence about one execution, while an invariant argument covers all executions allowed by the model.
guide.example:
P Q | P AND Q | P implies Q
F F | F       | T
F T | F       | T
T F | F       | F
T T | T       | T

Door states: Locked, Unlocked
unlock: Locked -> Unlocked, requires valid_key
lock: Unlocked -> Locked
Invariant: unlock succeeds only if valid_key is true.
guide.explanation: The implication is true when P is false because it forbids only a true premise with a false conclusion. For the door model, inspect every transition into Unlocked: the listed unlock transition requires a key. If a new emergency transition bypasses that guard, the proof must include it and the invariant may fail. A proof is only as complete as its model.
guide.exercise: Build the truth table for NOT(P AND Q) and compare it with (NOT P) OR (NOT Q). Then add a maintenance transition to the door that requires admin=true. State a corrected authorisation invariant covering both routes.
guide.solution: The two expressions match in all four rows: T,T,T,F for FF,FT,TF,TT. The revised condition is that unlock requires valid_key OR admin, with each transition enforcing its own guard.
guide.challenge: An account starts balance=0. Deposit adds a nonnegative integer; withdraw subtracts an integer only when 0<=amount<=balance. Prove balance>=0 is invariant, then identify a guard removal that invalidates the proof.
guide.challenge_solution: Base: zero is nonnegative. Deposit preserves it by adding a nonnegative value. Withdraw preserves it because amount<=balance. Removing that upper bound permits a negative balance. State integer/nonnegative assumptions explicitly rather than silently changing the model.

M02.concept: Logic gives precise meaning to claims. A proposition is true or false; a conjunction requires both parts, while an implication says that whenever its premise holds, its conclusion must hold. Sets collect elements, functions map inputs to outputs, and graphs represent relationships using vertices and edges. These tools make security policies less ambiguous.
M02.mechanism: A state machine describes possible states and the transitions between them. An invariant is a property that must hold in every reachable state. To prove one by induction, show it holds initially and that each permitted transition preserves it. Testing several states can find a counterexample but does not replace reasoning over all permitted transitions.
M02.example: Model a document as private or shared, with read and share operations. Define the invariant: only an owner may change sharing. List every transition and the required actor. Find a transition that would violate the invariant if its permission check were omitted. Express the corrected rule as a condition over the actor and document owner.
M02.pitfall: An implication does not assert its premise. 'If administrator, then may edit' does not mean everyone who may edit is an administrator.

check.question: What makes a property an invariant of a state machine?
choices: It held during one successful demo
It holds initially and is preserved by every permitted transition
Its name contains the word secure
check.explanation: Initial truth plus preservation establishes the property across all reachable states covered by the model.

guide.bridge: Builds on M02 proof assumptions and M01 division. Work examples by hand before reading number-theory notation.
guide.teaching:
Modular arithmetic identifies integers with the same remainder after division by a positive modulus. Writing a≡b mod n means n divides a-b. With a 12-hour clock, 14 and 2 represent the same remainder. Addition and multiplication respect this equivalence, so intermediate results may be reduced without changing the final remainder.

Division needs care. A modular inverse of a is a value x such that ax≡1 mod n. It exists exactly when a and n have greatest common divisor 1. Ordinary division and modular inversion are not interchangeable. The Euclidean algorithm repeatedly takes remainders to compute the greatest common divisor; its steps can be reversed to find an inverse.

Counting depends on whether order and repetition matter. Three independent slots with two choices each give 2×2×2=8 sequences. Choosing two people from three without order gives three pairs, not six. Before applying a formula, state the outcome space. Later cryptographic arguments rely on these assumptions; a large-looking number is meaningless if the choices are predictable or correlated.
guide.example:
Find inverse of 3 mod 7:
7 = 2*3 + 1
1 = 7 - 2*3
So (-2)*3 ≡ 1 mod 7; -2 ≡ 5 mod 7.
Check: 3*5 = 15 ≡ 1 mod 7.

But 2 has no inverse mod 6:
2*x mod 6 is always 0, 2 or 4, never 1.
guide.explanation: An inverse lets you undo multiplication only within the stated modulus. In the second case, common factor 2 prevents reaching remainder 1. For counting, list all two-bit sequences 00,01,10,11: order is visible because 01 and 10 differ.
guide.exercise: Calculate (8+11) mod 7 and (8*11) mod 7. Find the inverse of 2 mod 5 by enumeration. List all unordered pairs from {A,B,C,D} without repetition.
guide.solution: Remainders are 5 and 4. The inverse is 3 because 2*3=6≡1 mod 5. Pairs are AB,AC,AD,BC,BD,CD: six outcomes.
guide.challenge: Does 4 have an inverse mod 9? Show a check. Count length-three binary strings and unordered two-element subsets of a three-element set. Explain the difference in assumptions.
guide.challenge_solution: Inverse is 7 since 4*7=28≡1 mod 9. Binary strings: 8 ordered sequences with repetition. Two-element subsets: 3 unordered selections without repetition. These counts answer different questions.

M03.concept: Modular arithmetic wraps integers around a fixed modulus. On a twelve-hour clock, 10 + 5 is congruent to 3 modulo 12. A prime has exactly two positive divisors. Integers a and n are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1. This relationship determines when a has a multiplicative inverse modulo n.
M03.mechanism: Counting describes how many possibilities exist before assigning probabilities. Independent choices multiply: four positions with ten choices each give 10,000 strings when repetition is allowed. Cryptographic arithmetic uses very large spaces, but a large number alone is not a security proof. The algorithm, assumptions, and adversary's abilities also matter.
M03.example: Compute 5×3 mod 7 = 1, so 3 is an inverse of 5 modulo 7. Compare this with 2 modulo 6: multiplying 2 by any integer cannot produce a remainder of 1. List the possible remainders to see why. Then count four-digit strings with and without repeated digits, explaining why the formulas differ.
M03.pitfall: Ordinary division cannot simply be copied into modular arithmetic. An inverse may not exist.

check.question: Does 2 have a multiplicative inverse modulo 6?
choices: Yes, every nonzero number has one for every modulus
Yes, its inverse is the decimal number 0.5
No, because 2 and 6 are not coprime
check.explanation: An inverse must be an integer residue whose product is 1 modulo 6. None exists because gcd(2,6)=2.

guide.bridge: Builds on M03 counting and M02 sets. Fractions and conditional statements are the required mathematics.
guide.teaching:
Probability assigns weights to an outcome space. Conditional probability P(A|B) asks about A after restricting attention to cases where B occurs. Independence means learning B does not change A's probability; it is an assumption to justify, not a synonym for events having different names.

A base rate is the frequency of the condition before considering a test. Even a sensitive detector can produce mostly false alarms when true incidents are rare. Use counts to avoid confusing P(alert|incident) with P(incident|alert). Precision asks what fraction of alerts are real; recall asks what fraction of real incidents alerted.

Entropy measures uncertainty under a distribution. For a fair bit it is one bit. Two equally likely independent bits have four equally likely outcomes and two bits of entropy. Four possible labels do not imply two bits if one label dominates. Predictable random-number seeds can make generated values unsuitable for security even when their printed distribution looks varied.
guide.example:
Population: 10,000 events
Real incidents: 100; benign: 9,900
Detector catches 90 incidents and alerts on 99 benign events.
                  alert  no alert
incident            90       10
benign              99     9801
Precision = 90/(90+99) ≈ 47.6%
Recall    = 90/(90+10) = 90%
guide.explanation: The detector has high recall but less than half the alerts are true incidents because benign events are much more common. The denominator of precision is all alerts; the denominator of recall is all incidents. An accuracy near 99% would obscure this operational burden. Whether the tradeoff is acceptable depends on the cost of misses and reviews.
guide.exercise: Use a second population: 1,000 events, 20 incidents, 15 detected incidents and 35 false alerts. Fill all four matrix cells, calculate precision and recall, and state the number of missed incidents.
guide.solution: TP=15,FN=5,FP=35,TN=945. Precision=15/50=30%; recall=15/20=75%; misses=5. Every row and column must sum consistently to 1,000.
guide.challenge: A detector is applied to 100 events, including 10 incidents. It catches 8 incidents and alerts on 18 benign events. Calculate precision, recall and total alerts. Explain why independent trials would be an unsafe assumption for repeated events from one device.
guide.challenge_solution: Precision=8/26≈30.8%; recall=80%; alerts=26. Events from one device may share configuration or a single incident and be correlated. Treating them as independent can overstate the amount of evidence.

M04.concept: Probability describes uncertainty under stated assumptions. Conditional probability asks about an event after learning another event occurred. Independence means learning one event does not change the probability of the other; it cannot be assumed just because two events have different names. Entropy measures uncertainty in a distribution, not the visual complexity of a string.
M04.mechanism: Security alerts must be interpreted alongside the base rate of actual incidents. A highly accurate detector can still produce mostly false alerts when malicious events are rare. Build a count table rather than relying on phrases such as '99% accurate'. Separate the true-positive rate from the probability that a positive result is malicious.
M04.example: Among 10,000 events, suppose 10 are malicious. A detector catches 9 and falsely flags 1% of 9,990 benign events, about 100. Only about 9 of 109 alerts are true positives. Check each denominator and explain how the answer changes if the population contains many more malicious events.
M04.pitfall: A detector's sensitivity is not its precision. Both depend on which population and threshold are being measured.

check.question: In the worked example, approximately what fraction of alerts are true positives?
choices: 8 percent
90 percent
99 percent
check.explanation: There are about 9 true alerts and 100 false alerts. Precision is 9/(9+100), about 8%.

guide.bridge: Builds on M04 probability and P05 tests. This bridge introduces sampling distributions before OpenStax confidence intervals; no calculus is required.
guide.teaching:
A population is the group you want to describe; a sample is what you measured. The mean is sum/n. Sample variance divides squared deviations by n-1 when estimating population variance under standard independent-sampling assumptions. Standard deviation returns to the original units; standard error describes uncertainty in an estimator, not variability among individual observations.

Imagine repeatedly drawing samples of the same size and computing their means. Those means have a sampling distribution. A normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped model described by a mean and standard deviation. Under appropriate conditions, averages can be approximately normal, but tiny, biased or strongly dependent samples do not become trustworthy just because a formula is available. With known population standard deviation sigma and a suitable normal model, a mean interval uses mean ±1.96*sigma/sqrt(n). When sigma is estimated, t methods and their assumptions matter instead.

A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It is not a 95% probability that this particular fixed parameter moves inside this observed interval. A p-value concerns data at least as extreme under a null model, not the probability the null hypothesis is true. Choose metrics and splits before examining results, and preserve a held-out set against tuning.
guide.example:
Times (ms): 2, 4, 6
mean = 12/3 = 4
squared deviations = 4, 0, 4
sample variance = 8/(3-1) = 4 ms^2
sample standard deviation = 2 ms

Known-sigma teaching case:
mean=100, sigma=10, n=100
standard error=10/sqrt(100)=1
95% normal interval: [98.04, 101.96]
guide.explanation: The first calculation describes a tiny dataset and does not justify a population inference by itself. The second explicitly assumes a known sigma and an appropriate sampling model. Reusing sample standard deviation as if it were known population sigma hides uncertainty. Neither interval corrects a sample collected only from unusually fast machines.
guide.exercise: Calculate mean and sample variance for [1,3,5]. For TP=12,FP=3,FN=8,TN=77 calculate precision and recall. Write two reasons events collected repeatedly from one host might violate independent representative sampling.
guide.solution: Mean=3, sample variance=4, precision=12/15=80%, recall=12/20=60%. Shared configuration and temporal dependence are two plausible concerns; sampling only one host also limits generalisation.
guide.challenge: Before comparing two synthetic rules, write a protocol: use the fixed matrix results A=(TP=18,FP=12,FN=2,TN=68), B=(TP=16,FP=4,FN=4,TN=76). Choose whether precision or recall matters more, calculate both and defend a choice. Critique “p=0.03 means the hypothesis is 97% likely true.”
guide.challenge_solution: A: precision60%,recall90%; B: precision80%,recall80%. A misses fewer incidents but produces more false alerts. Choice depends on declared costs, not a universally best score. A p-value is conditional on the null model and does not give its posterior probability. Include sampling unit, fixed held-out data and uncertainty limits in your protocol.

M05.concept: A sample is the data observed; a population is what you want to understand. Sampling bias arises when the selection process systematically excludes relevant cases. An average hides variation, so report distributions or suitable summaries alongside it. A confidence interval quantifies uncertainty under assumptions about how the data were produced; it does not repair biased measurement.
M05.mechanism: Experiments compare a treatment with a baseline while controlling alternative explanations. Decide the hypothesis, metrics, datasets, and stopping rule before looking for a favourable result. In detection work, precision asks how many alerts are correct; recall asks how many malicious events were found. A change can improve one while worsening the other.
M05.example: For a labelled set with 20 malicious events, a detector finds 15 and produces 5 false alerts. Compute recall as 15/20 and precision as 15/20. Now add 15 false alerts without changing the true positives: recall stays fixed while precision drops. Document the dataset's source and why its event mix may differ from production.
M05.pitfall: More decimal places do not mean greater certainty. Measurement quality and sample design determine what a result supports.

check.question: A detector finds the same malicious events but doubles its false alerts. What happens?
choices: Recall increases and precision stays the same
Recall stays the same and precision decreases
Both necessarily increase
check.explanation: Recall depends on true positives and missed malicious events. Extra false positives reduce precision without changing recall.

guide.bridge: Builds on P06 programs, M01 binary and L02 the shell. Use a local C compiler from the linked CS50 setup, not a production machine configuration change.
guide.teaching:
C source is text. A compiler translates it, and a linker resolves references to libraries to produce an executable. A syntax error stops translation; a runtime error happens after the program starts. Read compiler diagnostics rather than treating successful compilation as evidence of correct behaviour.

A type determines representation and permitted operations. Integer sizes depend on the type and implementation; do not assume every int is the same size everywhere. sizeof reports bytes for this implementation. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than its maximum value; signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so it is not a portable wraparound technique.

Bytes have addresses and an order in memory. Endianness concerns the ordering of bytes within a multi-byte value, not the order in which you write ordinary decimal digits. Compile with warnings enabled and keep examples small enough to trace. Undefined behaviour can appear to work in one build, then change under optimisation; a single output is not a language guarantee.
guide.explanation: UINT_MAX is the implementation's largest unsigned int. Adding unsigned 1 wraps to zero by the language rule. The %zu conversion matches sizeof's size_t type. Replacing the unsigned variable with a maximum signed int and overflowing it would remove the portable guarantee; do not infer signed behaviour from this result.
guide.exercise: Compile the supplied program and record compiler version, command, warnings and output. Draw how the number 0x0102 would occupy two bytes under little-endian and big-endian conventions. Do not claim sizeof(int) is universal.
guide.solution: Little-endian: lower address 02 then 01; big-endian: 01 then 02. Unsigned wrap prints zero. The observed size belongs to the recorded platform.
guide.challenge: Explain each stage from source to execution. In an explicitly eight-bit unsigned model calculate 250+10; then explain why that result cannot automatically be asserted for signed char in a real C program.
guide.challenge_solution: The model gives 260 mod256=4. Signedness and representation rules differ; signed overflow is not defined as modular arithmetic. A full answer separates the mathematical model, C guarantees and observed implementation.

C01.concept: C makes the relationship between source code and machine execution more visible. A compiler translates source into object code, and a linker combines objects and libraries into an executable. Types determine how values are represented and which operations are meaningful. A declaration is a promise to the compiler, not automatic validation of external input.
C01.mechanism: Integer widths and signedness matter. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo a power of two; signed overflow in C is undefined behaviour. Undefined behaviour means the language does not promise a particular result, so an observed wraparound cannot be relied upon. Enable compiler warnings and understand each warning before treating a successful build as correct execution.
C01.example: Compile a program that prints sizeof values for selected integer types and reports the limits from the standard headers. Compare a safe boundary calculation with an intentionally avoided overflowing expression. Record compiler version and flags. Explain which observations come from this platform and which properties come from the language specification.
C01.pitfall: A program compiling without errors does not prove memory safety or correct arithmetic.

check.question: May portable C code rely on signed integer overflow wrapping around?
choices: Yes; all C integers wrap identically
Yes; a successful compilation guarantees it
No; signed overflow has undefined behaviour
check.explanation: Unsigned wrapping is defined, but signed overflow is undefined. Optimisations may assume it never happens.

guide.bridge: Builds on C01 compilation and P03 indexing. Use the same local compiler and disposable files.
guide.teaching:
An array is a contiguous sequence of elements. For char name[4], valid indices are 0 through 3. A C string additionally needs a zero byte marking its end. Three visible characters plus the terminator fill four bytes; the terminator is data occupying a real position.

An array does not carry a universal runtime bounds check. A function receiving a pointer generally needs a separate capacity contract. Reading beyond the last element is a defect even when it does not immediately crash. Distinguish input byte count, allocated capacity and visible character count, especially when using UTF-8.

A safe interface checks available capacity before copying and reports failure explicitly. Truncation is not always acceptable: truncating an identifier could select a different account or resource. Decide whether to reject, truncate or resize based on the application's meaning. Do not use a successful print as proof that the buffer was large enough.
guide.explanation: The comparison rejects a source whose visible byte length leaves no room for the terminator. Copying strlen+1 includes the terminator. This small example assumes src is already a valid terminated string; strlen itself cannot safely validate an arbitrary unterminated buffer.
guide.exercise: Run with src="cat", then src="cats", then src="". Predict output and exit status before each run. Draw all occupied indices for each accepted input.
guide.solution: cat prints and returns 0. cats is rejected with status 1 and no copy. Empty input stores only a zero byte and prints an empty line. No case should read or write beyond dst[3].
guide.challenge: A destination has capacity 6 bytes. Decide whether ASCII inputs "hello", "planet" and "" fit as terminated strings. Explain why a five-character Unicode string may still fail this byte-capacity check.
guide.challenge_solution: hello fits exactly with its terminator; planet needs7 bytes and is rejected; empty needs1. UTF-8 characters can occupy multiple bytes, so visible character count does not establish byte length.

C02.concept: An array stores a fixed sequence of elements. A C string convention uses a zero byte to mark its end; the terminator occupies space too. An array of four bytes can hold three single-byte characters plus a terminator. Text encodings complicate length: a character perceived by a reader need not occupy one byte.
C02.mechanism: A buffer's capacity, the number of bytes currently used, and the length of decoded text are different quantities. Check bounds before writing and account for terminators and encoding expansion. A function receiving a pointer cannot usually infer the original array's capacity, so pass sizes explicitly and document whether a size includes the terminator.
C02.example: Draw a four-cell buffer containing c, a, t, and zero. Attempting to append another character requires a fifth cell for a new terminator. Rewrite the operation to check required capacity before modifying anything. Repeat with a non-ASCII UTF-8 word and count bytes separately from displayed characters.
C02.pitfall: A null terminator is a byte value, not the same concept as a null pointer. Confusing the two leads to incorrect boundary reasoning.

check.question: How much capacity does the C string "cat" require with its terminator?
choices: At least four bytes
Exactly three bytes
One pointer-sized cell regardless of contents
